articles.title: Watch live: Red, Flight & Blue — The Future of U.S. Aviation
articles.summary: As the U.S. gears up for a record holiday travel season, the aviation industry is preparing to carry millions of passengers and thousands of tons of air cargo across the globe. Airlines are adapting and evolving to meet this growing demand as they navigate numerous headwinds like rising fuel costs, frequent government shutdowns and outdated…
articles.body:
As the U.S. gears up for a record holiday travel season , the aviation industry is preparing to carry millions of passengers and thousands of tons of air cargo across the globe.

Airlines are adapting and evolving to meet this growing demand as they navigate numerous headwinds like rising fuel costs , frequent government shutdowns and outdated infrastructure .

Congress is deliberating several proposals to alleviate these challenges, add certainty to the system, and deploy innovative technology the bring U.S. aviation into its next era. They include a proposed $30 billion overhaul of the U.S. air traffic control system that’s been years in the making. The ideas at play in Congress today have the potential to shape flight for years to come.

Join The Hill in partnership with Airlines for America as we bring together industry leaders, lawmakers, and stakeholders for a discussion on this critical moment in aviation as the industry gears up for one of the busiest seasons of the year.

We’ll discuss the opportunities and challenges facing the industry and imagine what’s possible for the future of flight.

The event is scheduled to begin at 8:30 a.m. EST.

articles.title: Duckworth to introduce bill requiring modernization of Pentagon’s ATC systems
articles.summary: Sen. Tammy Duckworth (D-Ill.) will introduce legislation on Wednesday that proposes requiring the Pentagon to modernize its air traffic control (ATC) systems, her office shared exclusively with The Hill. The “One Sky Act,” would require the Defense Department to produce a “risk assessment” of its ATC systems, and to develop a “modernization plan,” according to…
articles.body:
Sen. Tammy Duckworth (D-Ill.) will introduce legislation on Wednesday that proposes requiring the Pentagon to modernize its air traffic control (ATC) systems, her office shared exclusively with The Hill.

The “One Sky Act,” would require the Defense Department to produce a “risk assessment” of its ATC systems, and to develop a “modernization plan,” according to a one-page summary of the bill.

The risk assessment would consider “potential costs, timelines, and barriers” to modernizing the Pentagon’s ATC systems, which “desperately” need upgrading, Duckworth’s office said — citing a 2018 report to Congress from the Defense Department.

“It’s been no secret that we need to overhaul and modernize our air traffic control system. But as the FAA works toward this goal, the Pentagon cannot fail to keep up and widen an already existing safety gap,” Duckworth told The Hill. “We all fly in the same sky. And we need everyone to be on the same page. This commonsense bill would help ensure that our nation’s air traffic control modernization is a comprehensive effort to keep our skies safe.”

Within 180 days of the One Sky Act becoming law, the Defense secretary would have to submit the assessment and plan to address risks to the House and Senate Armed Services committees, per the bill’s text.

The Defense secretary would also have to submit annual reports to the two committees on the status of the ATC modernization efforts.

Duckworth, an Army veteran who lost both of her legs in the Iraq War, is a member of the Senate Armed Services panel. The Illinois senator is also the top Democrat on the Senate Commerce Subcommittee on Aviation, Space and Innovation.

Duckworth is scheduled to speak with The Hill’s Julia Manchester at 9:35 a.m. EST on Wednesday, during the paper’s “Red, Flight, Blue: The Future of U.S. Aviation” event .

Bryan Bedford, the administrator of the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), will also speak to Manchester during the event, which is sponsored by Airlines for America.

Bedford’s appearance will come less than a week after a widespread FAA outage led to the first nationwide ground stoppage since January 2023, and the subsequent cancellation of thousands of flights.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy has asked Congress for $50 billion to upgrade the nation’s ATC system in the wake of the ground stop.

Republican lawmakers previously allocated $12.5 billion to the FAA for upgrades via the 2025 One Big Beautiful Bill Act .

Duckworth’s office, though, said the Defense Department must also update its own ATC systems in a “joint effort” alongside the FAA.

The Illinois Democrat’s office stressed the need for the Pentagon to review its ATC systems, referencing the fatal crash in January 2025 between American Airlines Flight 5342 and an Army Blackhawk helicopter over the Potomac River and “several alarming near-miss events between military and civilian aircraft” since then.

“The safety of our servicemembers and the flying public demand we take these steps to keep the U.S. the global gold standard of military and civilian aviation,” the summary of the bill concluded.

articles.title: US infrastructure crumbles as adversaries power up – leaving Americans dangerously exposed: cyber expert
articles.summary: A wave of tech failures highlights weaknesses in America’s aging infrastructure that adversaries could exploit with increasingly accessible cyberattack tools, experts warn.
articles.body: A string of technology failures that left flights grounded and disrupted workplace software and banking systems is renewing concerns about weaknesses in America's critical systems foreign adversaries could exploit, according to experts. Cybersecurity professionals warn that U.S. adversaries are closely watching how the country responds to such failures for weaknesses they could exploit. A disruptive cyberattack doesn’t necessarily require sophisticated tactics, they say, and America’s foes already have the capabilities to carry one out. The National Security Agency on Tuesday experienced disruptions to internal systems during scheduled maintenance, though officials said its critical national security functions remained operational. Apple joined the wave of tech companies experiencing problems on Tuesday impacting services including the App Store, Apple Music and iCloud sign-ins. The tech giant attributed the disruptions to an internal update, saying many systems have since been restored. DUFFY: INVESTIGATORS EXAMINING 2 ROUTERS AFTER NATIONWIDE FAA GROUND STOP, NO SIGNS OF FOREIGN CYBERATTACK One day earlier, a technology failure forced United Airlines to delay departing flights by over 90 minutes. There was no indication of a cybersecurity issue. The latest disruptions followed Friday's nationwide ground stop triggered by the Federal Aviation Administration, which lasted over four hours, the longest in 25 years, creating travel disruptions that took airlines days to resolve. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said on "Fox News Sunday" there was no indication of a foreign cyberattack, stating that investigators are examining if faulty equipment or an installation problem triggered the hours-long ground stop. "We think it was the installation or the router that was the bad actor," Duffy said. "But we're open, if we see something else, we're gonna continue to investigate with our federal partners and law enforcement." According to The Wall Street Journal, FAA radio sites in El Dorado, Arkansas, and possibly Amarillo, Texas, overloaded the communications system used by air-traffic controllers. FAA SAYS AIR TRAVEL SHOULD BE BACK TO NORMAL SUNDAY AFTER NATIONWIDE GROUND STOP Meanwhile, a Microsoft Outlook outage on Thursday lasted for nearly 24 hours before service was restored Friday morning. Microsoft executive Charles Lamanna said the issue was the result of a previously undetected software defect, increased traffic and reduced server capacity. DAVID MARCUS: WHAT BIG TECH’S WEEKEND FROM HELL MEANS FOR THE FUTURE OF DATA CENTERS Also on Friday, Workday — whose human resources and payroll software is used by millions of Americans — experienced a widespread outage. "Workday is currently unavailable," a message for users said. "We are experiencing a service interruption. Your service will be restored as quickly as possible." PERPETUAL PARALYSIS: WHY EVERYTHING IS GRINDING TO A HALT On Monday, customers of several large banks — among them Chase, Bank of America and Wells Fargo — reported problems accessing online banking services. FOLLOW THE FOX TRUE CRIME TEAM ON X Chase acknowledged that some transactions were experiencing delays but noted that customers continued to have full access to their accounts and funds. BILL GATES SOUNDS ALARM ON AI-POWERED CYBERATTACKS, WARNS OF 'NEGATIVE SURPRISES' WITHIN A YEAR While officials have said there is no indication Friday’s ground stop was caused by a foreign cyberattack, U.S. adversaries have the capability to deliberately disrupt American infrastructure, Charles Tango, chief strategy officer at cybersecurity company Hydden, told Fox News Digital. He said any of America's adversaries have the capability to deliberately cause a disruption to the nation's infrastructure, and warned it's easier to pull off than many think. "It does not take a lot of sophistication these days to cause this type of attack, especially with the advent of AI, it's made security attacks much easier and much cheaper, but absolutely other countries like China would have immense capability of impacting our environments," Tango said. "They've spent a lot of time and a lot of effort trying to compromise our critical infrastructure." "Not all warfare needs to be kinetic these days. A cyber warfare can be very effective. We've seen that with Russia and Ukraine. We should be very mindful of the capacities that our adversaries have when it comes to cyber capability. Many of them specialize on offensive cyber capabilities, and that's what we should be focusing on," Tango said. "Other countries like China would have immense capability of impacting our environments. And we've seen that recently with organizations like Volt Typhoon," he added. CHINESE HACKERS TARGET NASA AND KEY US AGENCIES, DOJ ALLEGES Tango said aging systems, some within U.S. critical infrastructure, create vulnerabilities that capable adversaries can exploit, pointing to how a small equipment problem triggered a widespread disruption. CLICK HERE FOR MORE FROM THE FOX TRUE CRIME HUB "What we saw here is that one very small incident led to a widespread outage. That's because a lot of these systems are old. They've been around for a while. We haven't invested in upgrading them. And that's not just for the FAA. That's across critical infrastructure," Tango said. SEND US A TIP "I mean, the world is watching how we respond to this, and certainly our adversaries are watching this very, very closely," he added. HACKERS COULD ALREADY BE INSIDE AMERICAN UTILITIES, CYBER EXPERTS WARN OF 'TROJAN HORSE' THREAT The threat from foreign adversaries extends well past aviation. In 2024, federal cybersecurity agencies warned that Chinese state-sponsored hacking group Volt Typhoon had compromised U.S. energy providers and other critical infrastructure organizations. Officials assessed the group was positioning itself to be able to disrupt essential services during a conflict or major crisis with the U.S. LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST Michael Balboni, a former New York homeland security adviser who also served as a New York Power Authority trustee and is currently president of Adelphi University, told Fox News Digital that reports of foreign adversaries accessing American power grids have long concerned officials. WATCH: Former homeland security official discusses vulnerabilities in US infrastructure GET BREAKING NEWS BY EMAIL "We had reports and information that, in fact, adversaries were in the grids across the country," Balboni told Fox News Digital. "And that, again, had been there for years. The question becomes, what is their capability?" CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "Imagine taking out all the traffic lights in a major city," he said. "Imagine having the power go off to a hospital. Now, most hospitals have generators, but what if they don't come back on?"

articles.title: Sanders to push sweeping Medicare for All plan in next Congress
articles.summary: Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) plans to push a sweeping Medicare for All universal health care plan atop the Democratic agenda when he is expected to become chairman of the Senate Health, Education, Labor and Pensions (HELP) Committee next year. Sanders revealed his plan in an interview with The Associated Press, telling the news service that…
articles.body:
Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) plans to push a sweeping Medicare for All universal health care plan atop the Democratic agenda when he is expected to become chairman of the Senate Health, Education, Labor and Pensions (HELP) Committee next year.

Sanders revealed his plan in an interview with The Associated Press, telling the news service that universal health care is “no longer a utopian vision” but is “where the American people are,” citing sweeping Democratic victories in the midterm election.

Sanders’s plan would implement a universal health care system over four years. His plan would lower the Medicare eligibility age from 65 to 55 in year one and expand the program’s coverage to include dental and vision care, according to the AP. It would also guarantee health care for children up until age 18.

Sanders’s ambitious proposal would lower the Medicare eligibility age to 45 in its second year and to 35 in its third year. It would extend coverage to all Americans by year four.

The Vermont senator is viewing the budget reconciliation process as a way to get universal health care past a Republican filibuster in the Senate, although it would certainly be vetoed by President Trump if it managed to pass Congress.

The Hill reached out to Sanders’s office and the HELP Committee for confirmation.

Speaker Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) on Tuesday endorsed expanding Medicare to cover more Americans, arguing “we should lower the age of Medicare eligibility.”

Some incoming Senate Democratic freshmen, such as Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan and Troy Jackson of Maine, also support Medicare for All.

Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.), who is challenging Sen. Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) to become Senate majority leader in 2027, also supports Medicare for All but he says he would let the caucus decide its position on the sweeping proposal instead of forcing his own views on colleagues next year.

Some Democrats, however, haven’t fully embraced the idea yet, such as Sen.-elect Chris Pappas (D) of New Hampshire.

Asked about Medicare for All last week, Pappas told The Hill: “I want every American to be covered with health insurance” but added his top priority is to stop an estimated $1 trillion in Medicaid cuts from going forward.

“Right now we got to stop the cuts from going into effect. That’s the first order of business,” he said. “I hope that’s part of the early push next year.”

The Republican-controlled House Budget Committee estimates that Medicare for all would increase federal spending by $32 trillion over 10 years.

Medicare’s trustees in June projected the Hospital Insurance Trust Fund would become insolvent by 2033 unless reforms are made.

Sanders is scheduled to hold a press conference Tuesday morning on Capitol Hill about the HELP Committee’s 2027 agenda.

images.caption: Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) speaks to reporters alongside Sen. Elissa Slotkin (D-Mich.) during a press conference on Tuesday, November 10, 2026, to state they’re not supporting Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) for Majority Leader in the upcoming leadership election for the 120th session of Congress

articles.title: What to know about Ring Drone Cam, which can patrol your home for $250
articles.summary: Ring's Drone Cam flies room to room with AI navigation, 2K video and a $249.99 price, but it still awaits FCC authorization before it can ship in the U.S.
articles.body: Ever leave the house and suddenly wonder whether you closed the back door? You pull up your security camera, but it only shows the driveway. Not much help when you want to see what's happening inside. Well, Ring thinks it has an answer. And this one actually flies. Amazon-owned Ring has unveiled the Ring Drone Cam, a tiny $249.99 indoor security camera that flies from room to room. It can investigate security alerts, check specific areas of your home and send live video directly to your phone. Earlier this month, the company announced the new drone as part of its new Ring Robotics lineup. And thanks to artificial intelligence, it can navigate your home without someone steering it around. We also talked in depth about this new technology on "The CyberGuy Report Podcast," including what a flying camera could mean for home security. But before you get too excited about having your own miniature security patrol, there are some things worth knowing. Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the replay and discover 5 ways to travel smarter and save money. Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, 5 Ways to Travel Smarter and Save Money, has ended, but you can still watch the full replay. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways to protect your phone and personal information, avoid common travel scams, find better deals, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed. Watch the free replay + downloadable checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com. AI ROBOT MAY STOP YOUR DOG FROM BARKING WHILE YOU'RE GONE How Ring Drone Cam flies around your home Traditional home security cameras have one obvious limitation. They only show what's in front of them. Ring wants to change that. The Ring Drone Cam uses a system called AI Pilot to learn the layout of your home. During the initial setup, you carry the drone through your space while it creates a digital floor plan. From there, the system identifies rooms and suggests places worth checking. For example, maybe you want to see whether a window is open. Or perhaps your security system detects movement near the back door. You can save those locations in the Ring app. Then, when you want a closer look, the drone can fly there automatically. You can also create customized routes and schedule patrols with a compatible Ring subscription. The drone can work with connected Ring cameras and security sensors. If a linked device triggers an alert, Ring Drone Cam can automatically fly to a previously selected location to investigate. According to Ring's official announcement, AI Pilot combines cameras with onboard sensors and cloud processing to navigate around obstacles. So, instead of wondering what triggered an alert, you could actually see what's happening in another part of the house. Ring Drone Cam records 2K video as it flies The Ring Drone Cam weighs approximately 5.8 ounces and packs quite a bit of technology into its compact design. It records video at 1920 by 1920 resolution, which Ring describes as 2K. The camera has a 148-degree field of view and can rotate to capture a 360-degree view of a room. You can watch live footage through the Ring app. And if something happens at night, the drone has two built-in LED spotlights that illuminate dark areas. Unlike some traditional security cameras, it doesn't use infrared night vision. The drone also makes noise while flying. That's intentional. Ring says the audible propellers help people know when the camera is moving around. The drone has no microphone or speaker, so you cannot hear what's happening or talk to someone through it. There's also no built-in siren. And although it can move independently, it doesn't stay airborne indefinitely. Ring advertises up to eight minutes of flight time on a fully charged battery under controlled conditions. When the flight ends or the battery runs low, the drone returns to its charging dock. The man behind Ring has been working on this for years If this concept sounds familiar, there's a good reason. Ring originally announced a flying indoor security camera called the Always Home Cam back in September 2020. It was an ambitious idea at the time. Instead of installing cameras throughout your house, you could use one device to check different rooms. Ring founder and chief inventor Jamie Siminoff explained the thinking behind that original concept. In his September 2020 announcement, Siminoff wrote: "We wanted to create one camera that could give users the flexibility of every viewpoint they want around the home." However, bringing that concept to a broad consumer launch took much longer than expected. More than six years later, Ring is returning to the idea with a new product called Ring Drone Cam. This version uses AI to map your home, navigate around obstacles and fly to specific locations through the Ring app. In the company's November 2026 announcement, Siminoff explained what customers had been asking for. "For years, customers told us they wanted eyes in the places a fixed camera couldn't reach." The new drone reflects that feedback. Ring announced the original Always Home Cam at $249.99 in 2020. The new Ring Drone Cam carries that same advertised price in 2026. So, despite years of development and the addition of AI navigation, the announced price hasn't changed. That's pretty remarkable for a product with this kind of technology. WHAT A SMART FIREWALL DOES AND WHY IT MATTERS ON HOME WI-FI Can Ring Drone Cam really navigate around everything? Ring says its AI Pilot system can recognize obstacles and adjust its flight path as it moves. However, certain surfaces can make navigation more difficult. According to Ring's official product information, highly reflective floors, large mirrors and transparent glass can interfere with navigation. Rooms with plain walls and few visual details may also create challenges. The drone is limited to single-floor operation at launch, although Ring plans to support multiple floors in the future. It also requires Wi-Fi and a suitable location for its charging dock. Ring recommends an upload speed of at least 5 Mbps for optimal performance and 10 Mbps for 2K video quality. What about privacy with a flying camera inside your house? Ring says it has built several privacy protections into the device. Ring says the new Drone Cam only records while flying. When it returns to its docking station, the camera stops recording and the device powers down. A visible indicator and audible propellers help let people know when the drone is operating. The company also says recordings will receive protection through its new Throw Away the Key encryption system, known as TAKE. According to Ring's privacy documentation, the company retains video encryption keys for up to 24 hours to support enabled features. It then deletes its copies of those keys, leaving customers with control of the keys needed to access their recordings. However, TAKE differs from traditional end-to-end encryption because it allows Ring to process video for certain connected features during that initial period. There's another consideration. AI Pilot uses cloud processing as part of its navigation system. So, anyone thinking about buying one should understand how Ring handles the home's digital map and what information gets processed remotely. And if you share your home with someone else, it's worth discussing whether they're comfortable with a flying camera operating indoors. What Ring Drone Cam costs beyond the $250 price Here's something else to keep in mind before deciding whether this little drone belongs in your home. The advertised price is $249.99. That includes the drone and its charging dock. However, some features require a compatible Ring subscription. For example, you need a subscription to schedule automatic patrols. You'll also need a compatible plan if you want to save recordings in the cloud and review them later. Without a subscription, you can still use Live View to check what's happening. But if you want the drone to maintain a video history, there will be an additional recurring cost. Ring says eligible plans can provide up to 180 days of cloud video history, depending on the subscription and settings. And there's one more thing to consider. The drone relies on its battery for flight. With a maximum advertised flight time of eight minutes, you'll need to allow time for recharging between patrols. That makes it better suited for checking specific areas than watching your entire house continuously. FLOCK CEO, TECH RIVALS CALLED TO TESTIFY BEFORE SENATORS OVER AI CAMERA PRIVACY CONCERNS When can you buy a Ring Drone Cam? Ring says the Drone Cam is scheduled to begin shipping in the U.S. on January 27, 2027. The announced price is $249.99. However, the company still needs authorization from the Federal Communications Commission. So far, Ring says the device has not received the required FCC authorization and cannot legally be offered for sale or lease until that approval arrives. For now, you can sign up for product availability updates through Ring's official website at ring.com/products/drone-cam. And if you're wondering whether it will actually fly around your house as smoothly as it does in promotional videos, that's something we'll have to evaluate when the product becomes available. Kurt's key takeaways I have to say, I love the idea of a security camera that can actually fly through your home. If I'm away and something triggers an alert, I'd much rather send a camera to check it out than wonder what's happening beyond the view of my existing cameras. And at $250, Ring has certainly priced this to get people's attention. What I'm curious about is how well it actually flies through a home. Can it navigate doorways and avoid obstacles reliably? And then there's the privacy question. I'd want to know exactly how Ring handles the map of my home and who can access the footage. I'm looking forward to seeing this technology in action. We also talked about it in depth on my podcast, The CyberGuy Report at cyberguy.com/podcast. Check it out and subscribe for more conversations about the latest technology changing our lives. Would you let an AI-powered drone fly through your house to keep an eye on things, or would a camera that can roam from room to room feel like too much surveillance? Let us know by writing to us at CyberGuy.com. Sign up for my FREE CyberGuy Newsletter CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Copyright 2026 CyberGuy.com. All rights reserved.

articles.title: Nvidia rejects Huang offer to return as CEO
articles.summary: Nvidia does not plan to reinstate Jensen Huang, despite the former CEO’s suggestion that he would be “honored” to return if the company’s board of directors supported the move. Harvey Jones, Nvidia’s new chair, said Tuesday evening that the board “unanimously accepted his resignation and does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO.” Huang, who…
articles.body:
Nvidia does not plan to reinstate Jensen Huang, despite the former CEO’s suggestion that he would be “honored” to return if the company’s board of directors supported the move.

Harvey Jones, Nvidia’s new chair, said Tuesday evening that the board “unanimously accepted his resignation and does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO.”

Huang, who resigned last week in the wake of a series of affair scandals , said earlier Tuesday that he had received an “outpouring of calls” from some the firm’s staff, investors, business partners and customers for his return.

“NVIDIA is a once-in-a-generation company,” he said in a statement. “If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO.”

Huang stepped down after admitting to an affair with a woman who U.S. officials suspected of working as a Chinese intelligence asset . The board tapped longtime chief financial officer Colette Kress to take over as interim CEO.

But several prominent tech figures have called for Huang’s return, including Tesla CEO Elon Musk, Uber co-founder Travis Kalanick, Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney and Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan. President Trump has also signaled support for a comeback.

They joined more than 170,000 signatories in an open letter, urging the board to “bring Jensen back while an independent investigation establishes the facts” and arguing Huang “deserves due process, not mob justice.”

Jones’ comments came during Nvidia’s earnings call Tuesday. Despite the upheaval, the company posted strong third-quarter results , reporting $115.8 billion in revenue from July through September. This was up 20 percent from the previous quarter and 103 percent from the same time last year.

Despite the numbers, Democrats have pushed back on the tech mogul’s potential return.

articles.title: Rubio: ‘Zero’ evidence recent outages linked
articles.summary: Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Tuesday there is “zero evidence” that the recent string of technology outages are connected. “The first thing I want to make very clear is that we have zero evidence whatsoever, we have no indication, no evidence and no reason to believe at all that any of these incidents are…
articles.body:
Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Tuesday there is “zero evidence” that the recent string of technology outages are connected.

“The first thing I want to make very clear is that we have zero evidence whatsoever, we have no indication, no evidence and no reason to believe at all that any of these incidents are related to each other,” Rubio told reporters while in the Philippines.

“In essence, the Microsoft incident has nothing to do with what we saw with the [Federal Aviation Administration]; the FAA has nothing to do with what we saw with the banks a few days ago,” he continued. “These issues that have — we’ve seen from a technical standpoint are completely unrelated one from another.”

The secretary of state added, “That is what we have seen. That’s what all the evidence indicates.”

Department of Homeland Security (DHS) Secretary Markwayne Mullin cast the blame on rapidly developing artificial intelligence — which the Trump administration rebranded to “super intelligence” (SI) — citing a recent discussion with an unidentified person in the tech industry.

“I started talking to the tech industry,” Mullin told Fox News, stating he talked with an expert who thinks it is tied to AI because “these programs aren’t designed to work as fast as SI is.”

“When they put in a program that’s able to write codes and it goes in, it self-fixes itself,” the DHS chief added. “It’s like doing a change order on a house.”

He continued, “When you change one thing in a house, everything else starts changing, that’s a ripple effect. And it causes a system to be overran that weren’t designed to run as fast as the SI technology is today.”

Expansive tech issues — spanning from delayed and canceled flights after Friday’s nationwide ground stop to a previous Microsoft outage to interruptions in the banking system and beyond — have raised questions in recent days. President Trump, Vice President Vance and others in the administration have largely brushed off the concerns.

images.caption: U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio speaks to the press at the Solaire Resort near Manila, Philippines, Wednesday, Nov. 18, 2026.(AP Photo/Mark Schiefelbein) CORRECTION: Corrects the name of the location to the Solaire Resort, instead of the Solar Resort.

articles.title: British hackers face prison for GTA 6 data breach and crypto thefts | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Two British hackers face lengthy prison sentences for hacks that broke into the Grand Theft Auto gamemaker and for stealing millions in crypto.
articles.body:
Two British hackers are facing lengthy prison sentences for separate hacks as part of their roles in long-running, prolific cybercriminal hacking groups. The two are accused of hacks that stole millions of dollars in cryptocurrency and leaked pre-release footage from Grand Theft Auto VI.

Tyler Buchanan, 24, from Dundee, Scotland, has been sentenced to six years by a U.S. court after he was extradited to the United States in 2025. Buchanan was accused of stealing at least $11 million in cryptocurrency from dozens of companies as part of a phishing scheme. The attacks would impersonate IT helpdesks and call up unsuspecting employees and trick them into giving over their credentials, which the hackers would use to break in and steal cryptocurrency.

Meanwhile, Arion Kurtaj, 21, from Oxford, England, has pleaded guilty to several cyberattacks that he carried out while a teenager. One hack included the theft of data and extortion of Rockstar Games, the maker of Grand Theft Auto VI, which was released Wednesday after several delays .

Kurtaj was previously ordered by a U.K. court to be detained indefinitely after deeming him unable to stand trial due to his autism diagnosis and his perceived high hacking risk to the public. But U.K. authorities, tasked with charging Kurtaj with cybercrime offenses, confirmed Monday that he had admitted to several hacks, including leaking footage of the long-awaited video game, and would subsequently face a public trial.

U.K. authorities confirmed earlier reporting that Kurtaj hacked several companies, including while he was confined to a hotel amid police protection from rival criminal gangs. The authorities said Kurtaj used an Amazon Fire TV stick to hack the companies, which breached his bail conditions.

Both Buchanan and Kurtaj were members of overlapping cybercriminal groups, dubbed 0ktapus, Lapsus$, and later Scattered Spider . These prolific hacking gangs mostly consist of teenagers and young male adults, lending to the term “advanced persistent teenagers,” whose focus and motivations were to steal as much money as possible through various cyberattacks.

Over the years, the hackers were collectively responsible for hundreds of cyberattacks targeting big companies, including Coinbase , DoorDash , Mailchimp , and Nvidia .

By late 2024, both U.K. and U.S. authorities say they had indicted five of the hackers whom they believed were key members of the hacking groups, including Buchanan. The U.S. Department of Justice said this week that Buchanan is the fifth and final defendant to be sentenced in this case.

articles.title: Key House Republican pours cold water on $50 billion FAA funding ask
articles.summary: Rep. Steve Womack (R-Ark.) on Wednesday pushed back on the Trump administration’s $50 billion funding request for the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) in the wake of last week’s nationwide ground stop. During The Hill’s “Red, Flight & Blue: Future of U.S. Aviation” event, Womack told The Hill’s Sarah Fortinsky he is “skeptical” about the request…
articles.body:
Rep. Steve Womack (R-Ark.) on Wednesday pushed back on the Trump administration’s $50 billion funding request for the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) in the wake of last week’s nationwide ground stop.

During The Hill’s “Red, Flight & Blue: Future of U.S. Aviation” event, Womack told The Hill’s Sarah Fortinsky he is “skeptical” about the request and needs more information from administration officials before he can support it.

“We need a better plan, a sequential plan, some granular data that helps us understand what’s driving these costs,” added the Arkansas Republican, a member of the House Appropriations Subcommittee on Transportation, Housing and Urban Development.

After an FAA telecommunications outage led to the first nationwide ground stop since January 2023, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy asked Congress for $50 billion to upgrade the country’s outdated air traffic control (ATC) system .

Duffy had previously asked lawmakers for $30 billion. GOP lawmakers last year appropriated $12.5 billion for ATC upgrades via the One Big Beautiful Bill Act .

FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford reiterated the administration’s funding request at the event on Wednesday, saying the country’s ATC system is “unsustainable.”

“We need to build a system for the future that is going to allow us to continue to grow and expand,” Bedford told The Hill’s Julia Manchester.

But Womack said lawmakers first want answers on what caused Friday’s outage, questioning whether a cyberattack was behind it.

“I want to be able to isolate exactly what the issue was,” he said.

“We do need to be able to understand exactly what happened, so that we can prevent the same [thing] from happening, and then be able to continue to execute the plan that was already established,” the Arkansas lawmaker added.

articles.title: Instagram’s ‘school safety’ push was also a way to get more teens on the app
articles.summary: Internal documents reveal that Meta’s program to make Instagram safer for kids also served as a way to get more teens on the app, as reported by NPR.
articles.body: Meta’s initiative to make Instagram safer for schools stemmed from efforts to increase user “acquisition,” “friending,” and “invites,” according to a report from NPR. Internal documents revealed as part of a group of child safety lawsuits against Meta reference a “Project Gryffindor” — a school program that would “fuel organic and unattributed acquisition” of users. One internal presentation from November 2023 says a school program would “give teens a new reason to join / find more value in IG [Instagram].” The internal documents suggest Meta considered more goals than just teen safety when rolling out Instagram’s School Partnership Program, which launched touting features to fast-track moderation reports from participating school districts. Meta expanded this program in September by creating dedicated channels where schools can share announcements with students and parents. It also adds school banners to profiles, as well as directories for clubs and teams. Meta spokesperson Liza Crenshaw said in an emailed statement to The Verge that NPR’s story “completely mischaracterizes a positive program that helps thousands of U.S. schools protect their students online, communicate with them safely about extracurricular activities, and easily report safety issues.” Crenshaw adds that Meta doesn’t “want Instagram to be a distraction during class.” The November 2023 document says that Meta’s “current strategy of relying on power user teens to get less active friends onto IG may not be effective if there are full communities of teens that have not yet joined IG.” Another 2023 presentation questions whether Meta can “use school networks as a lever for acquisition,” and says that structured school data could “help improve the ability to find friends and acquaintances,” for attracting teens who “don’t think their friends are on IG.” In 2024, Meta started automatically putting users under 18 into more restrictive teen accounts while facing global scrutiny about the safety of its platforms. It later agreed to impose age verification, time limits, and an option to turn off personalized feeds to settle claims that its platforms are addictive.

articles.body:
Today, more than 7 million Americans are living with Alzheimer’s disease — a number projected to reach more than 13 million by 2050.

Each year, more Americans lose their lives to Alzheimer’s than to breast cancer and prostate cancer combined, and women bear a disproportionate share of that burden.

The condition is often associated with late-stage decline, but many people diagnosed early continue to live full lives. Although FDA-approved blood tests exist, a recent survey conducted by HealthyWomen found that only 13 percent of women ages 45-64 are aware of them — despite 90 percent expressing interest in taking one.

Awareness is not the only barrier to access: Medicare is not authorized to cover blood tests cleared for Alzheimer’s screening. To bridge this gap, bipartisan lawmakers have introduced the Alzheimer’s Screening and Prevention Act (ASAP), which would make blood screening tests available under the federal insurance program.

Join The Hill, in partnership with HealthyWomen, for a policy briefing featuring lawmakers, health experts, patients and advocates as we discuss the survey and expanding access to early Alzheimer’s testing.

The event features This is ALZ, a HealthyWomen campaign highlighting the real experiences of people living with the earlier stages of the condition.

The event is scheduled to begin at 12:30 p.m. EST.

articles.title: Sununu says airline prices won’t fall soon amid Iran war
articles.summary: Editor’s Note: This article was updated to reflect Sununu’s roles. Chris Sununu, president of Airlines for America and former governor of New Hampshire, said airline ticket prices will not go down any time soon at The Hill’s Red, Flight and Blue: The Future of Aviation event on Wednesday. Sununu said geopolitical challenges from the Iran…
articles.body:
Editor’s Note: This article was updated to reflect Sununu’s roles.

Chris Sununu, president of Airlines for America and former governor of New Hampshire, said airline ticket prices will not go down any time soon at The Hill’s Red, Flight and Blue: The Future of Aviation event on Wednesday.

Sununu said geopolitical challenges from the Iran war has caused airlines to eat the higher costs of oil, leading to higher costs for customers.

He said while ticket prices are high, the increase came off of a record low in prices, calling them “high, not higher.”

“Are they going to go down soon? No, they’re just not,” Sununu said.

He said the possibility of a government shutdown after the Dec. 11 deadline would cause more pain for the airline and air traffic control sectors.

“We obviously had this FAA glitch, they fixed it, and the American public needs to know that it’s safe and resilient and all that,” Sununu said. “And now you’re going to tell me you’re not going to pay your own air traffic control and TSA officers and all of that as we’re going into the holidays, I mean what a Grinch move that would be on behalf of Washington.”

The former governor said he is confident that “common sense” will prevail and Congress will avoid a shutdown. Sununu said the industry has been resilient but that airlines are struggling.

“Especially some of the smaller guys, they’re really getting crushed by these prices,” Sununu said. “At no fault of theirs, for geopolitical reasons, they’ve had to endure a lot on the cast side and ultimately their customers have had to do that as well.”

Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) is set to outline Senate Democrats’ healthcare priorities Wednesday morning, weeks after the party secured control of both chambers of Congress for next year.

Sanders, who is poised to chair the Senate Health, Education, Labor and Pensions Committee, is also expected to renew his push for Medicare for All. Democrats during the midterms leaned into addressing rising healthcare costs after the enhanced Affordable Care Act subsidies expired last year.

His remarks follow the Trump administration’s recent withdrawal of President Trump’s nominee to lead the Food and Drug Administration amid bipartisan opposition.

The press conference is scheduled to begin at 11 a.m. EST.

articles.title: Cassidy questions ‘odd’ White House move in pulling FDA nominee
articles.summary: Sen. Bill Cassidy (R-La.) questioned the Trump administration’s reasoning for pulling Food and Drug Administration (FDA) commissioner nominee Heidi Overton, saying he thought she had the support needed to be confirmed. “Tonight, the White House abandoned a viable confirmation path for Dr. Overton. The WH said that this was because she did not have the…
articles.body:
Sen. Bill Cassidy (R-La.) questioned the Trump administration’s reasoning for pulling Food and Drug Administration (FDA) commissioner nominee Heidi Overton, saying he thought she had the support needed to be confirmed.

“Tonight, the White House abandoned a viable confirmation path for Dr. Overton. The WH said that this was because she did not have the votes to pass. This was odd as I was having productive conversations with members,” Cassidy wrote on social platform X late Tuesday. “I believe she would have had the votes to pass out of committee and pass the full Senate.”

Cassidy, chair of the Senate health committee and a medical doctor, has been critical of many of the president’s nominees to lead U.S. health agencies, though he has ultimately supported them.

He had criticized Overton for supporting President Trump’s decision to recommend changes to the childhood vaccine schedule, but Cassidy said he had come around after she committed to “follow the science” in her role at the FDA.

“My conversations with her convinced me she would follow the science and push back against decisions that put Americans’ health at risk,” Cassidy said. “Unfortunately, with the limited time left, confirming a permanent FDA Commissioner will fall to Senate Democrats.”

Democrats are set to take a sizable majority in the upper chamber next year, an obstacle for Trump to nominate his preferred political appointees.

Trump nominated Overton back in August, and she was set to receive a critical vote in the Committee on Health, Education, Labor and Pensions on Wednesday. The White House confirmed to The Hill it pulled her nomination Tuesday evening.

Overton is a prominent health adviser in Trump’s orbit, leading the White House Domestic Policy Council. She is a prominent supporter of Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.’s Make America Healthy Again movement, and an opponent of abortion rights.

She drew criticism for a viral exchange while being questioned by senators where she would not answer whether the president was wrong about his past statements on vaccine safety.

Overton has remained anti-abortion and previously called the abortion drug mifepristone “dangerous,” Cassidy said senators were seeking assurances on the Trump administration’s commitments to the cause.

“The last issue was that pro-life Senators sought final assurances from the Administration regarding the Administration’s commitment to life issues,” Cassidy wrote Tuesday. “The Administration withdrew Dr. Overton rather than make such commitments.”

images.caption: Senate Health, Education, Labor and Pensions Committee Chairman Bill Cassidy (R-La.) greets Heidi Overton, President Trump’s nominee for the Commissioner of Food and Drugs (FDA), is seen before her nomination hearing on Thursday, September 24, 2026.

articles.title: Rogers will not seek waiver to remain top Republican on HASC
articles.summary: Rep. Mike Rogers (R-Ala.), chair of the House Armed Services Committee (HASC), will not seek a waiver from leadership to remain the top Republican on the panel, his office confirmed to The Hill late Tuesday. Republicans lost their majorities in the House and Senate during the midterms earlier this month. A Democrat, likely ranking member…
articles.body:
Rep. Mike Rogers (R-Ala.), chair of the House Armed Services Committee (HASC), will not seek a waiver from leadership to remain the top Republican on the panel, his office confirmed to The Hill late Tuesday.

Republicans lost their majorities in the House and Senate during the midterms earlier this month. A Democrat, likely ranking member Rep. Adam Smith (D-Wash.), will lead the committee starting in January.

Rogers, who won reelection against Democrat Lee McInnis, was seeking a waiver as House Republican rules limit lawmakers from being chair or ranking member of a panel past three terms. The waivers are granted by GOP leadership.

The Alabama Republican has been a top member on the committee since 2020.

Rogers’ decision, which was reported earlier by Punchbowl News, leaves GOP Reps. Trent Kelly (Miss.) and Ronny Jackson (Texas) to compete for the ranking member spot next term.

Rep. Rob Wittman (R-Va.), the vice chairman of HASC and chairman of the Subcommittee on Tactical Air and Land Forces, lost his reelection bid against Democrat Shannon Taylor in Virginia’s 1st District.

images.caption: Representative Mike Rogers, a Republican from Alabama and chairman of the House Armed Services Committee, during a hearing in Washington, DC, US, on Thursday, May 14, 2026. The hearing is meant to examine the agency’s 2027 budget request. Photographer: Eric Lee/Bloomberg via Getty Images
